tldr: When cameras and LiDAR cannot function in environments like darkness or smoke, this new state estimation framework, SBEE, prevents fatal vertical drift in legged robots by remembering contact heights as a terrain elevation map and feeding them back.
hero_caption: Overall view of the SBEE framework. An LI-EKF that updates base states from an IMU and leg kinematics is bidirectionally coupled with a grid elevation map accumulating foot contact heights. Terrain heights from previously visited cells are fed back to the filter as vertical pseudo-measurements.
overview:
When operating legged robots autonomously in dark, smoke-filled, or visually degraded environments, exteroceptive sensors like cameras and LiDAR cannot be trusted. The robot must rely entirely on proprioception: onboard IMUs, joint encoders, and contact force sensors. Under purely proprioceptive sensing, however, global position and yaw are mathematically unobservable.

Vertical (Z-axis) drift is especially catastrophic. Horizontal shifts merely translate the local reference frame without breaking locomotion, but a height error of just a few centimeters causes swing legs to strike the ground too early or miss contact entirely, triggering a fall.

To tackle this, the authors drew inspiration from how humans navigate in the dark. Even without vision, each step on the floor subconsciousnessly builds a mental map of elevation. When stepping on the same spot again, that memory anchors our height sense. Formulating this concept in a manner analogous to SLAM for legged robots led to SBEE (Simultaneous Base and Elevation Estimation).

SBEE couples a Left-Invariant Extended Kalman Filter (LI-EKF) for floating-base estimation with a local grid elevation map in a bidirectional loop. Every stable foot contact registers an uncertainty-aware height sample into the map. When the robot revisits a mapped cell, the stored elevation is fed back to the filter as an uncertainty-weighted vertical pseudo-measurement. This firmly checks vertical drift without requiring any external perception.

Evaluated in MuJoCo simulations on quadrupedal and bipedal platforms, and on the real-world ANYmal-D GrandTour dataset across 296 m in a Swiss canyon, SBEE cut absolute trajectory error (ATE) by 22.1% compared to the best of three state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators.
contributions: Formulating SBEE for the first time: building a local terrain elevation map from foot contact history and feeding previously visited terrain heights back to the filter as loop-closure vertical corrections.

Achieving a fixed-dimension (15D) Left-Invariant EKF that avoids augmenting contact point positions into the state vector, consuming a kinematic 3D velocity measurement instead, which decouples the state dimension from the number of legs and foot geometries.
Adopting a torus-indexed circular buffer that shifts the map center with zero memory copies, achieving real-time performance of 0.162 ms per cycle on an embedded board (Raspberry Pi 5).

sections.heading: Walking in the dark: recalling height through the soles of the feet
sections.summary: In extreme environments where exteroceptive sensors fail, state estimation must rely exclusively on proprioception. However, double integration of accelerations leads to severe vertical drift. This paper introduces a framework that treats the walked terrain itself as a persistent proprioceptive landmark to anchor the vertical axis.
sections.details:
Legged robots capable of traversing rough terrain and stairs are expected to play major roles in harsh environments unsuitable for humans, such as inspections and disaster sites. Maintaining stable balance requires high-rate, accurate base state feedback (position, orientation, and velocity).

When vision is compromised, the sole lifeline is proprioceptive sensing: IMUs, joint encoders, and foot force sensors. Under proprioception alone, however, the robot's global position and yaw are fundamentally unobservable. Above all, vertical (Z-axis) drift is fatal. Any minor error or bias in canceling gravity (1G) causes position errors to grow quadratically over time through double integration. If estimated height drifts upward, the robot expects the ground to be lower, driving swing legs too far down with high impact. If it drifts downward, the foot misses the ground when expected, causing an immediate fall.

The authors highlighted an overlooked insight: with every step, the robot observes foot contact height relative to its base frame. Similarly, humans walking in the dark subconsciously construct a mental map of floor elevation from tactile sensations under their feet. Returning to a previous spot, we anchor our sense of height with confidence.

Formulating this intuition into robotics yielded SBEE. The robot maintains stepped-on terrain as an external memory and uses it as a vertical anchor upon revisiting, suppressing vertical drift without exteroceptive sensors.

captions.F1: Conceptual diagram of terrain elevation mapping via foot contacts. With purely proprioceptive sensing, estimated height gradually drifts from ground truth (top-left). By accumulating contact heights into a map (bottom-left) and anchoring to this terrain, vertical error is kept within a bounded range (right).

sections.heading: Bridging prior gaps: invariant filtering meets tactile mapping
sections.summary: Legged state estimation has long relied on EKFs and Invariant EKFs (In-EKF) fusing kinematics and IMUs, but lacked persistent terrain memory. Meanwhile, proprioceptive terrain mapping existed only as an open-loop output, never closing the loop to correct base state estimation.
sections.details:
Proprioceptive state estimation and terrain mapping for legged robots have followed two distinct threads.

### II-A & II-B Leg Odometry and Invariant Kalman Filters
Classically, standard EKFs fusing kinematics and IMUs under the assumption of stationary stance feet (e.g., PRONTO, MUSE) have been widely used. Recently, Invariant Extended Kalman Filters (In-EKF) exploiting Lie group geometry have gained traction. Because the error dynamics become linear and autonomous (log-linear property) independent of the estimated state trajectory, they provide superior mathematical convergence stability. However, traditional contact-aided In-EKFs augment contact point positions for each stance leg into the state vector as random walks. As leg counts grow, the state dimension expands and tuning becomes difficult. Invariant smoothers also marginalize and discard past states outside a sliding window, preventing the reuse of terrain stepped on earlier.

### II-C Elevation Mapping and Proprioceptive Sensing
Representing the terrain beneath a robot as a 2.5D grid elevation map has been studied for years, but most methods rely on exteroceptive sensors like LiDAR or depth cameras. Although some works build elevation maps using proprioception alone, their goal was gait adaptation or geological analysis; the map was strictly an open-loop output of the base estimator.

### II-D Positioning and Contributions of This Work
This work unites both lines in a bidirectional loop for the first time. The state estimator updates the map, and the accumulated elevations in the map provide loop-closure corrections that bound vertical drift. By removing contact positions from the filter state, the fixed-dimension LI-EKF runs efficiently regardless of the number of legs or foot geometries.

sections.heading: Problem formulation: why vertical drift is catastrophic
sections.summary: Defining coordinate frames and notations reveals the unobservability of vertical position under proprioceptive sensing and its physical hazards. The overall execution flow shows how the SBEE framework addresses this challenge.
sections.details:
### III-A Coordinate Frames and Notations
Three primary frames are considered: the stationary inertial world frame $\{w\}$, the moving base frame $\{b\}$ attached to the robot chassis, and the foot contact frame $\{f\}$. Leading superscripts denote the expressing frame; for instance, base position in world frame is ${}^{w}\bm{p}_{b}$, and foot position in base frame is ${}^{b}\bm{p}_{f}$. The rotation matrix ${}^{w}\bm{R}_{b} \in \mathrm{SO}(3)$ transforms orientations from base to world.

### III-B Unobservability of Vertical Position and Physical Threats
Using only an IMU, joint encoders, and contact force sensors, the 3-axis global translation $({}^{w}p^{x}_{b}, {}^{w}p^{y}_{b}, {}^{w}p^{z}_{b})$ and yaw about the vertical axis are fundamentally unobservable. However, the operational impact across axes is highly asymmetrical. Horizontal (X, Y) drift simply translates the local reference frame, which modern feedback controllers can handle seamlessly.

Conversely, vertical $({}^{w}p^{z}_{b})$ drift is physically destructive. Legged locomotion controllers depend on knowing where the ground is. Recovering position from IMU accelerations requires double integration, rapidly accumulating small biases and gravity compensation errors quadratically over time. Kinematic constraints only tie the relative distance between base and feet; they cannot anchor global absolute elevation. When estimated base height drifts, swing legs either smash into the floor or sweep through thin air, causing an immediate loss of balance.

### III-C SBEE Processing Overview
To overcome this, SBEE couples an LI-EKF and an elevation mapper in a bidirectional loop:
- Step 1: Predict the LI-EKF state using IMU inputs.
- Step 2: Update the filter using base velocity derived from leg kinematics.
- Step 3: Insert height data into the local elevation map using base estimates and foot contact states.
- Step 4: Recenter and interpolate the map as the robot moves.
- Step 5: Read elevations from visited low-variance cells and correct filter vertical drift via pseudo-measurements.

Returning from unvisited terrain to previously visited ground produces an effect analogous to loop closures in SLAM.

sections.heading: Tactile elevation mapping: painting the ground through foot contacts
sections.summary: Rapid and reliable terrain maps are constructed using continuous contact confidence for foot height estimation, torus-indexed zero-copy grid management, 1D Kalman filter cell updates, and neighborhood propagation with interpolation.
sections.details:
### IV-A Contact Confidence Estimation
Traditional contact detection relied on force thresholds or Schmitt triggers (binary ON/OFF), which struggle with impacts, foot slippage, and payload shifts, demanding manual per-gait tuning. This work adopts a continuous contact confidence $CC_i \in [0, 1]$, computed by normalizing each leg's normal ground reaction force $F_i$ against the mean load across all legs. This smoothly scales observation reliability even during dynamic motions.

### IV-B Proprioceptive Terrain Sensing
The height of a stance foot in the world frame, $z = {}^{w}\bm{p}_{f}^{z}$, serves as an elevation measurement. The measurement variance $\sigma^{2}_{z}$ fed to the map is computed from encoder error propagation divided by contact confidence $CC_f$. Feet with less certain contact receive higher variance (lower confidence).

### IV-C & IV-D Torus Indexing and Map Recentering
The local terrain is maintained in an $M \times M$ square grid centered on the robot. Each cell stores elevation mean $h$ and variance $\sigma^{2}$. As the robot traverses near the boundaries, the map center must be recentered. Large-scale memory copying would cause latency spikes; instead, setting $M$ as a power of two enables torus indexing (circular buffer) via bitwise AND operations. This achieves $O(1)$ complexity, clearing out-of-boundary cells while preserving stored data without physical memory moves.

### IV-E Cell Updates and Loop Closure Effects
Cell elevations are recursively updated using 1D Kalman filters. Revisiting the same cell monotonically lowers variance $\sigma^{2}$, forging it into a rigid anchor. When a robot that has drifted vertically steps onto such a cell, the low variance yields a high Kalman gain, pulling the drifted base height back to ground truth. A lower variance clamp prevents overconfidence.

### IV-F & IV-G Neighborhood Propagation and IDW Interpolation
Updating only pinpoint contact locations leaves empty cells. For stable contacts (especially planar feet), the estimated surface normal $\bm{n}$ is used to project a local tangent plane across a neighborhood radius $r$ (neighborhood propagation). Between updates, Inverse Distance Weighting (IDW) fills unvisited gaps, drastically raising the odds that the next footstep lands on an already-informed cell.

sections.heading: Fixed-dimension LI-EKF: a geometric filter agnostic to leg count
sections.summary: Formulating the base state on the extended Lie group SE2(3) yields a 15-dimensional Left-Invariant EKF including IMU biases. Kinematic world base velocity acts as the measurement rather than augmenting contact states, maintaining a fixed state dimension and high convergence stability regardless of leg count.
sections.details:
### V-A & V-B State Space and Left-Invariant Error
The floating-base state is defined on the extended special Euclidean group $\mathrm{SE}_{2}(3)$. The state matrix comprises rotation $\bm{R}$, translational velocity $\bm{v}$, and position $\bm{p}$. Given true state $\mathcal{X}$ and estimate $\hat{\mathcal{X}}$, the left-invariant error is defined as $\bm{\eta}^{L} = \mathcal{X}^{-1} \hat{\mathcal{X}}$. Its perturbation vector $\bm{\xi} \in \mathbb{R}^9$ is expressed in the robot's local base frame.

Because the process dynamics satisfy the group affine property, the time evolution of the left-invariant error follows a linear differential equation dependent strictly on IMU inputs, independent of the estimated trajectory itself. This key property of invariant filtering prevents linearization breakdowns and yields robust convergence stability.

### V-C Prediction Step
In discrete-time propagation, covariance is advanced using a second-order truncation of the matrix exponential. This second-order coupling accurately accounts for physical error transitions: local attitude errors propagating to velocity errors, and velocity errors propagating to position errors.

### V-D Kinematic Velocity Update
Conventional contact-aided In-EKFs include contact point positions for each stance leg in the state, altering state dimension whenever legs make or break contact. This method avoids that. Solving the stance condition via forward kinematics and base angular velocity for each supporting leg, it synthesizes a single world-frame base linear velocity measurement ${}^{w}\bm{v}_{b}^{\mathrm{kin}}$, weighted by contact confidence $CC_f$. A world-frame velocity measurement perfectly matches the left-invariant formulation, yielding a state-independent measurement matrix. Consequently, the state dimension stays identical whether the robot has two or four legs.

### V-E & V-F IMU Bias Augmentation and Retraction
Gyroscope and accelerometer biases (3D each) are appended as Euclidean states, yielding a 15D augmented system $\mathrm{SE}_{2}(3) \times \mathbb{R}^6$. Although biases break strict group affinity, error dynamics Jacobians remain state-independent. Corrections computed at each update step are mapped back (retracted) onto the base state via right multiplication using the Lie group exponential map.

sections.heading: The SBEE framework: turning terrain data into a vertical anchor
sections.summary: Coupling the elevation map with the LI-EKF injects past cell heights into the filter as vertical pseudo-measurements. A Schmidt-Kalman partial update ensures map uncertainties never corrupt attitude, velocity, or bias estimates.
sections.details:
### VI-A Vertical Update from Terrain Elevation
When foot $f$ establishes stable contact ($CC_f \ge CC_{\mathrm{stable}}$), the framework queries the elevation map cell corresponding to its horizontal position, retrieving elevation $h_f$ and variance $\sigma_f^2$. The elevation innovation $z_{h,f}$ is the difference between this stored height and the predicted foot height from the current base state.

Here lies a critical design decision. Because the map acts as an external memory outside the Kalman state, it may carry unmodeled systematic errors. A full Kalman update could let elevation errors corrupt base velocity, attitude, or IMU biases, destabilizing the entire filter. The authors adopted a Schmidt-Kalman partial update: applying a selector matrix $\bm{\Gamma} = \mathrm{diag}(0, 0, 1)$ to the Kalman gain restricts updates strictly to the base world vertical position (${}^{w}p^z_b$).

Horizontal positions, velocities, attitudes, and IMU biases remain mathematically untouched. Even if the map is noisy, it can at worst introduce a slight height bias without ever crashing attitude or velocity loops. Being a 1D scalar update, it requires no matrix inversions, executing in microseconds.

### VI-B Execution Flow per Cycle
Each control cycle follows an organized routine (Algorithm 1):
1. Propagate the LI-EKF using IMU data.
2. Compute base velocity from leg kinematics and perform the LI-EKF velocity update.
3. Register stable foot contact heights into the elevation map using the latest base estimate.
4. Apply neighborhood propagation and IDW interpolation, recentering the map if needed.
5. Query cell heights at stable foot locations and apply the partial vertical update to the LI-EKF.

### VI-C Advantages of External Contact Memory
Decoupling contact states into an external map locks the state dimension to 15. The exact same code and parameters run on quadrupeds, bipeds, or future multi-legged robots without modifications. Foot geometries are handled uniformly just by tuning how measurements are inserted—a single point height for point feet, or local planar orientations for flat soles.

sections.heading: Experimental results: vertical drift slashed by 96%, traversing a 296 m canyon
sections.summary: Evaluated in MuJoCo simulations (quadruped Go2, biped G1) over rough ground and slopes, and on a 296 m ANYmal-D dataset in the Swiss Grindelwald canyon. Terrain updates cut vertical errors dramatically, reducing trajectory error by 22.1% against state-of-the-art proprioceptive baselines.
sections.details:
### VII-A Metrics and Setup
Simulation benchmarks evaluated 3D position/velocity RMSE, horizontal RMSE, vertical RMSE ($\mathrm{RMSE}_z$), accumulated vertical mean offset ($\bar{e}_z$), and attitude error against ground truth. To highlight the true impact of terrain feedback, no post-hoc trajectory alignment was applied.

### VII-B Simulation Evaluations (Quadruped Go2 and Biped G1)
- **Go2 Rough Terrain**: In blind locomotion over rubble with frequent slips and impacts, standalone LI-EKF without terrain updates drifted vertically by 0.89 m. Full SBEE held the vertical offset to just 0.019 m, slashing $\mathrm{RMSE}_z$ by 96.8%.
- **Go2 Slope**: Walking up a 10-degree incline (~1.0 m climb), the baseline failed to track ground rise and underestimated final height by 0.65 m (65% error). SBEE tracked within 0.02 m final error, lowering $\mathrm{RMSE}_z$ by 96.4%, demonstrating true 3D terrain tracking rather than an assumption of flat ground.
- **G1 Biped Slope**: Walking the humanoid biped G1 with flat feet up a similar slope yielded sparser contacts than a quadruped. However, neighborhood propagation of normal vectors from surface contacts allowed the map to converge rapidly. While the baseline overestimated height by 0.177 m over a 0.37 m climb, SBEE tracked with only 0.011 m error.

### VII-C ANYmal-D GrandTour Dataset Comparison
Real-world performance was benchmarked on CYN-1, a challenging outdoor dataset where ANYmal-D traversed the Grindelwald canyon in Switzerland across 296 m for 520 s. Comparisons were made against three state-of-the-art proprioceptive estimators from a recent benchmark: MUSE, contact-aided IEKF, and Invariant Smoother (IS).

- **Absolute Trajectory Error (ATE)**: SBEE achieved 1.062 m. This is a 22.1% improvement over the best baseline IS (1.364 m), 24.4% over IEKF, and 53.2% over MUSE. Across 296 m, the error rate was only 0.36% of distance traveled.
- **Velocity and Attitude**: Linear velocity RMSE was lowest at 0.0758 m/s. Relative pose error (RPE) over 1 m intervals showed the best rotational accuracy (0.5568 deg).
- **Trade-offs**: Over short 1-frame intervals, SBEE showed slightly higher RPE than IEKF. Continuous contact confidence shifts and strong vertical updates induce minor high-frequency variations. SBEE trades momentary smoothness for long-term drift suppression.

### VII-D Computational Load
Processing time was clocked on an Intel Core i7 desktop and a Raspberry Pi 5 (embedded target). One cycle required 0.025 ms on the i7 and 0.162 ms on the Pi 5. Enabling terrain updates only increased computation by 4% to 14%, leaving ample margin for robot control loops running at hundreds of Hertz to 1 kHz.

captions.F6: Base position estimation for quadruped Go2 during simulated slope walking. Without terrain updates (dash-dot line), the estimator loses track of the incline. SBEE with terrain updates (solid blue line) accurately tracks the true elevation profile (dotted line, ~1 m climb).
captions.F7: Visualization of the elevation map built by quadruped Go2 during slope traversal using proprioception alone. Without cameras or LiDAR, the 3D ramp shape is clearly reconstructed purely from foot contact information.
captions.F8: Position estimation for biped G1 during slope walking. Unlike the quadruped, the baseline drifts upward. SBEE firmly binds the vertical trajectory to ground truth regardless of drift polarity.

sections.heading: Discussion: why it works and what challenges remain
sections.summary: Analyzing the theoretical rationale behind SBEE's success (state-independent Jacobians, safe Schmidt-Kalman vertical coupling, low-cost torus buffers) alongside current assumptions (rigid ground surface, unobservable horizontal/yaw drift) and limitations.
sections.details:
SBEE's strengths stem from the precise synergy between geometric filtering and terrain representation, rather than a mere aggregation of isolated components.

- **Benefits of State-Independent Linearization**: Because the process model is group affine, error propagation Jacobians do not depend on the estimated trajectory. This preserves the physical validity of the propagated vertical covariance, allowing appropriate weighting against terrain elevation measurements.
- **Scalar, Safe Partial Coupling**: With Schmidt-Kalman updates, observation corrections map strictly onto the single world vertical position row via the base frame. They never touch attitude, velocity, or IMU biases. Even if the map encounters a sudden step error, the filter is theoretically protected from divergence.
- **Bounded Computation**: Torus indexing provides $O(1)$ memory shifts, and removing contact points from the state ensures a fixed state dimension that easily runs real-time on microcomputers.

Limitations remain clear:
First, terrain is assumed to be static, non-deformable rigid ground. On soft mud, snow, or shifting rubble, erroneous heights will be registered and persist until overwritten by future contacts.
Second, the method strictly bounds vertical (Z-axis) drift. Horizontal positions (X, Y) and global yaw remain unobservable under pure proprioception, meaning long-term drift is inevitable.
Third, simple vertical force ratios cannot directly identify lateral foot slippage. However, the contact confidence module is modular and can be replaced with advanced slip estimators.

sections.heading: Conclusion: closed tactile loops unlock vision-free autonomous locomotion
sections.summary: SBEE establishes a proprioceptive framework where legged robots build an elevation map from foot contacts and leverage it as a vertical anchor. It provides a robust foundation for continued locomotion even when exteroceptive sensors are lost.
sections.details:
This paper presented SBEE (Simultaneous Base and Elevation Estimation), enabling legged robots to construct terrain elevation maps from tactile contact and reuse them as vertical anchors to suppress vertical drift without exteroceptive sensors.

A local elevation map is maintained efficiently via torus indexing and updated through 1D Kalman filters and neighborhood propagation. A 15-dimensional LI-EKF queries this map, producing loop-closure corrections whenever the robot revisits high-confidence cells. Holding contact history in an external map rather than the filter state yields a versatile, lightweight architecture independent of leg count and foot shapes.

On the ANYmal-D canyon benchmark over 296 m, SBEE reduced absolute trajectory error by 22.1% against state-of-the-art proprioceptive baselines while running in just 0.162 ms per cycle on a Raspberry Pi 5. Slated for open-source release, this framework marks a major milestone toward blind autonomous locomotion in harsh, degraded environments.

sections.heading: Appendix: mathematical proof of state-independent left-invariant error dynamics
sections.summary: First-order perturbation expansion of a group-affine system proves that the left-invariant error dynamics do not depend on estimated or true trajectories, but strictly on IMU inputs.
sections.details:
This appendix outlines the linear derivation of the left-invariant error dynamics presented in equations (34)–(35).

The left-invariant error $\bm{\eta}^{L}_t = \mathcal{X}^{-1}_t \hat{\mathcal{X}}_t$ is expanded to first order with perturbation $\bm{\xi}_t \in \mathbb{R}^9$ as $\bm{\eta}^{L}_t \approx \bm{I} + \bm{\xi}_t^{\wedge}$. Applying the group affine property to the differential equation and neglecting second-order terms and noise-error cross products yields the blocks for rotation, velocity, and position:
- The rotation error derivative features a cross product with IMU angular velocity: $-[\bm{\omega}_t^{\mathrm{imu}}]_\times \bm{\xi}_t^R$.
- The velocity error derivative contains coupling with IMU acceleration: $-[\bm{a}_t^{\mathrm{imu}}]_\times \bm{\xi}_t^R - [\bm{\omega}_t^{\mathrm{imu}}]_\times \bm{\xi}_t^v$.
- The position error derivative includes local velocity error $\bm{\xi}_t^v$ and angular velocity coupling $-[\bm{\omega}_t^{\mathrm{imu}}]_\times \bm{\xi}_t^p$.

Applying Lie bracket identities back into vector form rigorously proves that the transition Jacobian $\bm{A}_t$ contains no estimated orientation $\hat{\bm{R}}$ or position $\hat{\bm{p}}$, depending purely on IMU measurements ($\bm{\omega}^{\mathrm{imu}}, \bm{a}^{\mathrm{imu}}$). This mathematical property provides the foundation preventing covariance collapse under aggressive motions.

takeaways: Treating foot contact heights as an external elevation map and reusing them as vertical pseudo-measurements dramatically bounds vertical drift using proprioception alone.
Using a synthesized 3D kinematic velocity measurement instead of augmenting contact states allows a fixed-dimension (15D) In-EKF that is independent of leg count and foot geometries.

Restricting elevation feedback strictly to the world vertical base position via Schmidt-Kalman partial updates theoretically prevents map errors from corrupting attitude, velocity, and bias estimates.
limitations: The rigid-ground assumption means elevation errors can occur in deformable terrain like mud and snow, or on shifting debris, persisting until revisited.
Only vertical (Z-axis) drift is bounded; horizontal position (X, Y) and global yaw remain fundamentally unobservable and prone to long-term drift under pure proprioception.
The vertical force-ratio contact confidence estimator cannot detect lateral slippage, requiring more advanced contact estimators on slippery surfaces.
